structure.title: Your app is inside the Pages folder
structure.text: app.js, package.json and node_modules are all sitting inside Pages/. That folder is only supposed to hold the html pages and the images folder. Move app.js and package.json up to the main project folder, next to Pages, and run npm install there. Then you start it with node app.js from the project folder and it serves the files in ./Pages.

structure.title: You have 2 package.json files
structure.text: I found them in: Pages/package.json, package.json. You only need one, at the top. This usually happens when npm init or npm install gets run in the wrong folder, and then it's not clear which one is the real project.

structure.title: You have 2 node_modules folders
structure.text: I found them in: Pages/node_modules, node_modules. Install once, in the folder that has package.json. Right now the same packages are stored twice.

structure.title: The package.json at the top doesn't say how to start the app
structure.text: It has no "main" and no "start" script, so node app.js or npm start from the top folder fails with "Cannot find module". I had to dig into Pages/ to find your app.

structure.title: Pages and Pages/images folders exist
structure.text: Found Pages/ and its images folder.

structure.title: The index page is called Index.html
structure.text: Rename it to index.html, all lowercase. On Linux and most web hosts file names are case-sensitive, so Index.html and index.html are different files.

tips: Your code keeps its own list of valid ISBNs. You don't need that. Just ask sendFile for the file and, if it isn't there, the callback gives you err.code === "ENOENT" and you can send "File Not Found". Then adding a book is only adding a file.

fb.ok: One route with a path variable handles every book and reads it from request.params. This is exactly the pattern the assignment is after.
fb.test: I scanned app.js for app.get routes: 1 with a path variable (/select/:x), 0 separate per-book routes; request.params used: yes.
fb.why: One route for every book is the core idea of the assignment: adding a book then means adding a file, not writing more code.

fb.fix: sendFile is used, but without the {root: ...} option. Passing the folder as root (instead of building a full path yourself) is the safer and more portable way, and it blocks requests such as ../ from escaping the folder.
fb.test: I looked for response.sendFile(file, {root: ...}) in the code.
fb.why: root keeps requests inside your Pages folder (so a URL like ../app cannot read other files) and avoids building the path by hand.

fb.fix: You used path.join. It also avoids hard-coding slashes, which is great. The assignment specifically asks for path.resolve, which turns the pieces into one absolute path.
fb.test: I looked for path.resolve(...) in the code.
fb.why: path.resolve gives one absolute path that works on Windows, Mac and Linux alike.

fb.ok: GET / returns your index page, and its three links go through your app (/select/ISBN) instead of pointing at the .html files.
fb.test: GET / returned 200. Index page (served at /) has 3 links of the form /select/ISBN and 0 direct links to .html files.
fb.why: Links that go through /select/ prove a click reaches your route; a direct .html link skips the app entirely.

items.item: The 3 book pages are served at /select/ISBN

fb.test: GET /select/014044792X returned 200; GET /select/0140449132 returned 200; GET /select/1685781152 returned 200.
fb.why: Each of your three proposal books must be reachable through the route.

items.item: A book that does not exist returns 'File Not Found'

fb.ok: A request for a book that does not exist answers "File Not Found".
fb.test:
GET /select/0000000000000 returned 404:

404 - Book Not Found

The ISBN 0000000000000
fb.why: A missing book is an expected case, not a crash, so it needs its own clear answer.

items.item: An unknown page returns a 'not found' response (separate handler)

fb.example:
// put this AFTER all your routes: it catches every address that matched nothing
app.use((request, response) => response.status(404).send("Page Not Found"));
fb.ok: An unknown address gets its own "not found" answer, separate from the missing-book case.
fb.test:
GET /no-such-route/xyz returned 404:

404 - Page Not Found

The page you requested does no
fb.why: An address that matches no route should get your own message, handled separately from a missing book.

fb.example:
// put this last, after the "Page Not Found" handler. The four parameters are what make it an error handler
app.use((err, request, response, next) => response.status(500).send("Server Error"));
fb.fix: I did not find a "Server Error" response. Add an error-handling middleware (four parameters: err, request, response, next) after your routes, and send "Server Error" from it.
fb.test: I forced two errors. GET /select/%E0%A4%A returned 400: Error</tit; GET /select/..%2Fapp returned 404: <h1>404 - Book Not Found</h1> <p>The ISBN ../app does n
fb.why: Anything unexpected must still end in a clean "Server Error" instead of a stack trace or a hanging request.

fb.ok: About 11% of the lines in app.js are comments, which makes the file easy to follow.
fb.test: 4 of 37 non-empty lines in app.js contain comments (11%). Full marks need 10% or more.
fb.why: Comments explain why the code is written the way it is, which helps you and anyone who reads it later.

items.item: Cover on each book page

fb.test: I looked for in the HTML of each book page: 3 of 3 book pages have it.
fb.why: The cover is part of the book page the assignment asks for, and the /images/ path is how the app serves it.
fb.ok: Every page has an cover tag.

fb.test: I compared the page text with the price in your proposal: 3 of 3 book pages have it.
fb.why: The price is one of the three things each book page must show.
fb.ok: Every book page shows the price from your proposal.

fb.test: I compared the page text with the title in your proposal: 3 of 3 book pages have it.
fb.why: The title is how a reader knows which book the page is about.
fb.ok: Every book page shows the title from your proposal.

items.item: Student name on each book page

fb.test: I looked for your name in the text of each book page: 3 of 3 book pages have it.
fb.why: The assignment asks for your name on the bottom of every page.
fb.ok: Your name appears on every book page.
